strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies 'mean-collapse' as a failure mode in perturbation prediction, connects it analytically to the MSE objective being dominated by non-responsive genes (Eq. 4), and aligns this with recent independent findings (Mejia et al., 2025).

The proposed method is coherent: perturbation-conditioned subgraph extraction (Gumbel-Softmax node selection combining structural GNN embeddings with LM-based semantic embeddings of the perturbed gene) plus an adaptive signal–noise loss (Huber penalty on non-DEG changes, DEG-aware alignment loss) directly targets the diagnosed failure mode.

Evaluation goes beyond global correlation: DEG-aware metrics (DES@K, Spearman-sig, LFC-weighted Spearman, direction match) and PDS are computed using a standardized framework (cell-eval), and results are stratified by perturbation effect size (Table 3), which directly probes the mean-collapse claim. Gains are largest precisely where mean-collapse is most severe (small-effect perturbations: +28% DES).

Reasonably thorough ablations: removing z_context or L_non degrades performance (Figure 4), and the effect-size-dependent behavior of λ_non (Figure 5) is an interesting and honest empirical observation.

Appendix provides substantial reproducibility material: dataset statistics (Tables 4–5), knowledge graph construction and filtering statistics (Table 6), metric definitions (Appendix B), baseline descriptions, and a hyperparameter search protocol with validation-based selection and no test leakage.
Pathway-level validation (GSEA on HIRA knockdown, Figure 10) adds biological plausibility evidence beyond numeric metrics.
weaknesses: Overstated claims of consistency: on RPE1, MorPH beats AdaPert on PDS (0.688 vs 0.663) and TxPert is essentially tied on DES@50 (0.242 vs 0.244), yet the abstract and Section 5 claim AdaPert 'consistently outperforms' baselines. Statistical significance is never tested; Tables 1/3 report std over test perturbations (not seeds), and the number of runs behind Table 2's std is unspecified.

Methodological novelty is moderate: the components (Gumbel-Softmax subgraph selection, Huber loss on non-DEG genes, cosine alignment to a DEG-derived target) are individually standard, and the core diagnosis and DEG-aware evaluation largely follow existing work (Mejia et al., 2025; Virtual Cell Challenge / cell-eval). The contribution is a sensible combination rather than a new technique.

Internal inconsistencies hurt confidence: Eq. 7 states the semantic embedding is computed with GPT-4o (which is not an embedding model), while Appendix A.3 says GenePT embeddings from OpenAI text embedding models are used — which is actually used is unclear. Figure 9's caption ('Top-10 predicted genes') does not match the described DEG-coverage-by-hop-distance analysis. Figure 8's caption mentions tertiles of mean absolute differential expression while the text defines effect size by fraction of DEGs.

Potential circularity/leakage needs clarification: training losses (Eq. 14, 16, 18) rely on per-perturbation DEG labels derived from ground-truth perturbed profiles. The paper should explicitly confirm these are computed only on training perturbations and discuss the inconsistency between the p<0.05 threshold used in training (no multiple-testing correction) and the FDR-based DES used at evaluation.

Limited benchmark diversity: only two datasets, both single-gene CRISPR knockouts from the same Replogle study; Norman et al. (2019) and Dixit et al. (2016) are cited but not evaluated, and no combinatorial perturbations, cross-cell-line transfer, or other modalities are tested, leaving generalization claims narrow.

Reproducibility gaps for the proposed method: a detailed hyperparameter search space is provided for the TxPert baseline (Table 8) but not for AdaPert itself (λ_non, λ_align, Gumbel temperature τ, selection threshold T, GNN depth, encoder/decoder architecture are not fully specified), and no code release is mentioned.

Some results are glossed over: the small-effect PDS slightly degrades relative to TxPert (↓0.4%, Table 3) without discussion; the pathway correlation r = 0.53 is moderate, and only 3 of 14 significant ground-truth pathways are significant in both analyses, yet the text describes pathway agreement quite positively.

strengths: The paper targets a real and well-motivated failure mode ('mean-collapse') in perturbation prediction, and the DEG-aware evaluation suite (DES@K, DE-Spearman, direction match) is well defined and more informative than global correlation alone.

The method is clearly described overall: differentiable Gumbel-Softmax subgraph extraction conditioned on perturbation semantics, plus a non-DEG Huber loss and subgraph alignment loss, is a reasonable and mostly coherent design.

The ablation studies (effect of z_context and L_non across effect-size regimes, Figure 4) and the effect-size-dependent sensitivity analysis of λ_non (Figure 5) add useful insight beyond a single aggregate number.

Baseline coverage is respectable, spanning both KG-free (scVI, CPA, STATE) and KG-based (GEARS, TxPert, MorPH) methods under a common split and evaluation protocol, with metric definitions provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Overclaiming relative to the evidence: Section 5.1 states AdaPert 'achieves the best performance on both datasets,' but MorPH has higher PDS on RPE1 (0.688 vs 0.663); Appendix F claims best performance 'across all reported metrics' on RPE1, yet CPA exceeds the proposed method on DES@100 (0.337 vs 0.320). Similarly, Table 3 shows AdaPert's PDS slightly decreases for small-effect perturbations (↓0.4%). These contradictions undermine the central 'consistently outperforms' claim.

Limited and homogeneous evaluation: only two datasets (K562 and RPE1 from Replogle et al., 2022), single-gene knockouts only, same experimental platform. No combinatorial perturbations (e.g., Norman et al.), no cross-cell-line generalization, and no external validation beyond a single HIRA knockdown case study.

No statistical rigor: differences over baselines (e.g., Pearson-∆ 0.619±0.262 vs 0.580±0.255) are small relative to the reported per-perturbation spread, and no significance tests or seed-level variance for the main tables are reported ('mean ± std over multiple runs' is ambiguous). Figure 1 rests on a single cherry-picked perturbation (UQCRB).

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned; key details are missing or inconsistent — the main text says perturbation embeddings come from GPT-4o (Eq. 7), while Appendix A.3 says GenePT Ada/Model-3 embeddings are used; the Gumbel temperature, subgraph size threshold T, and loss weights are not specified; Table 9 is referenced in the numbering sequence but absent.

Fairness of baseline tuning is questionable: Table 8, described as the 'hyperparameter search space used for the TxPert baseline,' actually contains AdaPert-specific components (DEG weight, Non-DEG Huber weight/δ, subgraph options), raising doubts about whether baselines received equivalent tuning effort.

The DEG sets D(p) driving both training losses and effect-size stratification are defined by an uncorrected p < 0.05 test on noisy single-cell data; the sensitivity of the method to DEG-set definition (e.g., FDR correction, threshold choice) is not analyzed, and the claimed novelty of identifying 'mean-collapse' is weakened by explicit reliance on prior findings (Mejia et al., 2025).

No limitations or research ethics discussion is provided, and the contribution is largely an incremental combination of known components (subgraph sampling, LLM embeddings, robust losses) rather than a new understanding or method class.

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a real and increasingly recognized failure mode (mean-collapse) in perturbation response prediction, motivating the method with a clear decomposition of the reconstruction loss (Eq. 4) rather than only anecdote; this connects to independent recent findings (Mejia et al., 2025).

The proposed method is coherent: perturbation-conditioned subgraph extraction via Gumbel-Softmax node scoring, combined with a non-DEG Huber penalty and a DEG-alignment loss, directly targets sparse perturbation effects; the design choices are well motivated.

Evaluation is more thorough than typical for this area: unseen-perturbation splits, standard baselines including recent KG-based methods (GEARS, TxPert, MorPH, STATE), DEG-aware metrics following the Virtual Cell Challenge protocol, effect-size stratification (Table 3), ablations (Fig. 4), sensitivity analysis of λ_non (Fig. 5), and pathway-level (GSEA) validation on HIRA knockdown.

Useful analyses such as DEG coverage as a function of graph hop distance (Fig. 9) empirically support the premise that local graph context is informative, and the effect-size-dependent behavior of L_non is a genuinely interesting empirical finding.
Appendix provides dataset statistics, KG statistics, metric definitions, and a hyperparameter search space, which helps reproducibility.
weaknesses: Benchmark diversity is limited: results are reported only on two datasets (K562.Replogle and RPE1.Replogle) from the same source (Replogle et al., 2022). Standard community benchmarks such as Norman et al. (2019) or Dixit et al. (2016) are absent, so generality of the claimed improvements is not established.

Gains over the strongest baseline (TxPert) are small or absent on RPE1 in Table 10 (DES@50 0.244 vs 0.242; DES@100 0.320 vs 0.314), yet the text claims 'ADAPERT achieves the best performance across all reported metrics' without any statistical significance testing. Similarly, Table 1 shows MorPH outperforms AdaPert on RPE1 PDS (0.688 vs 0.663), contradicting the claim that 'ADAPERT achieves the best performance on both datasets' on both metrics. No paired tests or multiple-run variance for the main tables (the number of runs behind 'mean ± std over multiple runs' is not stated), making it hard to judge whether differences are meaningful.

There is a degree of circularity in the adaptive learning scheme: D(p) is derived from statistical tests on training data, and the alignment loss directly supervises z_context toward a target built from ground-truth DEG effect sizes (Eqs. 18-20). While legitimate as training labels, this means the method is trained to reproduce exactly the quantity measured by the headline DEG-aware metrics, and no analysis (e.g., of the learned subgraphs against known biology) is provided to verify the 'biological structure' interpretation.

Methodological details are underspecified: the hard threshold 'α̃_v > T' applied to Gumbel-Softmax samples is not differentiable and T is never specified; the main text says descriptions are encoded with GPT-4o (Eq. 7) while Appendix A.3 says GenePT embeddings from OpenAI text embedding models are used — these are different components and the discrepancy is unresolved.

A key ablation is missing: given Fig. 9 shows most DEGs lie within 1-3 hops of the perturbed gene, a simple static k-hop neighborhood baseline (no learned subgraph selection) should be compared to isolate the benefit of the adaptive selection machinery over trivial local context. Additionally, the graph used is already aggressively preprocessed (HVG + top-k STRING edges), so the 'dense static graph' strawman being improved upon is partly the authors' own construction.

Hyperparameter selection uses Pearson-Δ as the primary metric (Appendix E), while the paper's central claims rest on DEG-aware metrics; this mismatch could disadvantage baselines on exactly the metrics where AdaPert claims its largest gains. Also, Table 8 is labeled as the search space 'for the TxPert baseline' yet contains AdaPert-specific losses (Non-DEG Huber weight, DEG weight), causing confusion about what was actually tuned for whom.

Table 3 lacks the std values its caption promises, small-effect results show a PDS regression (↓0.4%) that is not discussed, and the novelty is moderate (perturbation-conditioned subgraph sampling plus DEG-weighted losses are natural combinations of existing tools: Gumbel-Softmax, Huber loss, contrastive-style alignment), so the contribution rests heavily on empirical rigor — which is undermined by the inconsistencies above.
No statement of code availability or release, which is important for reproducibility given the many pipeline components (KG preprocessing, GPT-based embeddings, cell-eval integration).

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a real and practically important failure mode ('mean collapse') in perturbation response prediction, supported by recent independent findings (Mejia et al., 2025), and connects it cleanly to the sparse structure of perturbation effects (Eq. 4 decomposition).

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: four cell lines (K562, RPE1, JURKAT, HEPG2) under an unseen-perturbation split, strong and recent baselines (TxPert, MorPH, GEARS, STATE, CPA, scVI, plus linear and foundation-model probes), two independent evaluation protocols (cell-eval style metrics and Systema), effect-size stratification, DEG-definition sensitivity analysis (Appendix D), knowledge-graph source/density ablations (Appendix E), threshold sensitivity (Figure 24), and a downstream GSEA pathway case study (Appendix G).

The core ideas are sensible and well-motivated: perturbation-conditioned subgraph extraction via differentiable node selection, a Huber-style non-DEG suppression loss, and a DEG-alignment loss directly target the diagnosed failure mode; the ablations (Figures 4, 5, 23) show each component contributes, particularly for small/medium-effect perturbations where mean collapse is most severe.

Appendix evidence supports the design assumptions, e.g., DEG graph-proximity analysis (Figure 7) justifies local subgraph context, and the KG ablations (Figure 20) provide a useful empirical finding that node coverage and moderate edge density matter more than density.

The cross-cell-line experiment (Figure 13, Table 13) is honestly reported: simple baselines (Perturb Mean, Linear-GenePT) beat all deep models on Pearson-Δ there, and the authors acknowledge AdaPert is designed for the unseen-perturbation setting rather than claiming universal superiority.
weaknesses: Claim–table inconsistencies undermine confidence: Section 5.1 states AdaPert 'achieves the best performance on both datasets' for Pearson-Δ and PDS, but Table 1 shows AdaPert's RPE1 PDS (0.663) is below MorPH (0.688). Similarly, gains over TxPert on some metrics are very small (HEPG2 MAE-Δ −0.6%, RPE1 Overlap@50 +0.9%, DE Direction Match +0.8–1.9%) yet are summarized as consistent wins without statistical significance testing; std values reported are across perturbations, not runs, so no inference about whether differences are reliable is possible.

There is a potential circularity/leakage concern: the DEG sets D(p) derived from ground-truth perturbed data drive the training losses (Eqs. 14–21), and the evaluation metrics most emphasized (DES, DE-Spearman, Overlap@50) are DEG-based; the method is thus directly optimized toward the headline metrics. The DEG-threshold sensitivity analysis (Appendix D) partially mitigates this, but the paper does not compare against a baseline given the same DEG supervision (e.g., TxPert with a DEG-weighted loss), so the contribution of the subgraph mechanism versus simply reweighting the loss is not fully isolated.

Methodological details that affect reproducibility are underspecified or inconsistent: Section 3.3 says descriptions are retrieved from NCBI or generated by GPT-4o and encoded with an OpenAI text-embedding model, while Appendix A.3 uses precomputed GenePT embeddings; the Gumbel-Softmax 'sampling' followed by hard thresholding (α̃ > T, Eq. 12) is described as differentiable without explaining how gradients flow through the thresholding step; the number of runs behind 'mean ± std over multiple runs' (Table 2) is unstated; and no code release is mentioned despite heavy dependence on specific external resources (STRING version, GenePT/OpenAI embeddings, GPT-4o fallback).

The headline mean-collapse evidence (Figure 1) is a single perturbation (UQCRB) and the causal attribution to the MSE objective is argued analytically rather than demonstrated experimentally (e.g., no experiment showing that a plain autoencoder with a DEG-aware loss but no graph closes most of the gap, which would test the 'modeling vs. data' claim).

Methodological novelty is incremental: Gumbel-Softmax node selection, Huber losses, and DEG-weighted/masked objectives are standard components; the contribution is their combination with a perturbation-conditioned graph context, and the positioning against Mejia et al. (2025), who already identified the mode-collapse problem, could be sharper.

Some claims are asserted rather than supported, e.g., that knowledge-graph baselines 'propagate noise' and 'yield many false positives' is stated without direct measurement of false-positive rates on non-DEG genes for baselines (Figure 25 covers only three methods on one dataset).

strengths: The paper identifies and articulates a real, well-motivated failure mode (mean-collapse) in perturbation response prediction, supported by a recent independent finding (Mejia et al., 2025), and connects it to the sparse structure of perturbation effects (Eq. 4 decomposition is a clean framing).

Evaluation breadth is above average: four Perturb-seq cell lines under unseen-perturbation splits, a cross-cell-line transfer setting, an independent second evaluation protocol (Systema), pathway-level GSEA case studies, DEG-threshold sensitivity analysis (Fig. 19), KG-source/density ablations (Figs. 20-24), and per-effect-size stratification.

DEG-definition sensitivity analysis (Appendix D) and the attention-threshold analysis (Fig. 24) proactively address potential sources of bias, and the appendix provides unusually detailed dataset, KG, and metric definitions.

The cross-cell-line discussion is honest: the paper openly reports that Perturb Mean and even a linear probe outperform AdaPert on Pearson-Δ in that setting, and correctly scopes the method to the unseen-perturbation regime rather than overclaiming.
Metrics are aligned with community standards (cell-eval / Virtual Cell Challenge), which eases comparability with prior work.
weaknesses: Potential circularity between training supervision and evaluation: the model is trained with losses explicitly shaped by ground-truth DEG masks and effects (L_non on D̄(p), L_align on ΔX over D(p), Eq. 18), and is then evaluated primarily on DEG-aware metrics (DES, DE-Spearman, direction match) computed from those same DEG definitions. Improved DEG metrics may partly follow by construction rather than reflecting better perturbation-specific biology. An ablation of a simple DEG-mask/Huber-weighted loss on a non-graph backbone (without the subgraph machinery) is needed to isolate what actually drives the gains.

Gains over the strongest baseline (TxPert) are modest in absolute terms: Pearson-Δ 0.619 vs. 0.580 on K562 and 0.674 vs. 0.655 on RPE1, and the headline 'up to 28%' improvement corresponds to DES rising from 0.090 to 0.115. For small-effect perturbations, PDS actually decreases (0.740 to 0.737, Table 3). No statistical significance testing, no clear reporting of seed variance for AdaPert vs. baselines (Table 2's 'multiple runs' is ambiguous), so claims of consistent superiority are weakly supported given the reported std over perturbations is large.

Novelty is incremental: each component is a known technique (Gumbel-softmax node selection over a knowledge graph, Huber loss on non-responsive genes, cosine alignment to a DEG-derived target), and the mean-collapse phenomenon itself is already documented in cited work. The paper does not clearly demonstrate that the learned subgraphs are biologically meaningful beyond aggregate metrics — Fig. 24 provides only a single-gene (POLR2B) case study of node selection.

Methodological ambiguity undermines reproducibility: DEG definitions are inconsistent between the main text (Eq. 14, p < 0.05) and the appendix (BH-adjusted FDR < 0.05 with |LFC| > 0.25); key hyperparameters (λ_non, λ_align values, temperature τ, selection threshold T used for final results, number of layers) are not stated in the main methodology; and no code release is mentioned despite the heavy dependence on external APIs (GPT-4o, OpenAI embeddings) whose outputs are not reproducible.

Genes with missing NCBI descriptions are described using GPT-4o generations, a detail with leakage/quality implications (model-generated text could echo known perturbation effects) that is neither analyzed nor ablated.

Some evidence is internally inconsistent or overstated: the abstract claims outperformance 'across multiple benchmarks,' yet on RPE1 the best baseline (MorPH) beats AdaPert on PDS (0.688 vs. 0.663), and in the cross-cell-line setting AdaPert trails Perturb Mean by a wide margin. The writing also contains sloppiness (raw '~\cite{NCBI7381}' in Figure 3, 'Subraph' typo, overlapping text in Figure 1), suggesting insufficient polish for the main track.

strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies and formalizes 'mean-collapse' as a concrete failure mode in perturbation prediction, connecting it to the MSE objective's decomposition over responsive vs. non-responsive genes (Eq. 4), which gives the method a principled rather than purely heuristic justification.

Extensive and multi-protocol evaluation: four cell lines (K562, RPE1, JURKAT, HEPG2) under the unseen-perturbation setting, plus a cross-cell-line transfer setting, evaluated under both cell-eval metrics (Pearson-Δ, PDS, DES, Spearman, direction match) and an independent 'Systema' protocol, with consistent AdaPert wins on most headline metrics (e.g., Pearson-Δ and PDS across datasets in Tables 1, 9-12).

Comprehensive ablation and sensitivity analyses: DEG-threshold sensitivity (Appendix D), knowledge-graph source and edge-density ablations (Appendix E), attention-threshold sensitivity (Fig. 24), adaptive vs. fixed context comparisons (Fig. 23), and effect-size-stratified analysis (Table 3, Figs. 4-5) provide unusually thorough evidence for design choices.

Honest handling of limitations: the cross-cell-line setting shows AdaPert below Perturb Mean and Linear-GenePT baselines, and the paper candidly attributes this to the method being designed for unseen-perturbation transfer; the impact statement appropriately cautions against over-reliance on predictions.

The method components (differentiable Gumbel-Softmax subgraph selection, Huber-regularized non-DEG loss, DEG-aligned contrastive objective) are coherently combined and each ablation supports its role, particularly for small-effect perturbations where mean-collapse is most severe.
weaknesses: Improvements over the strongest baseline (TxPert) are modest and not uniformly consistent: per-metric wins alternate (e.g., TxPert leads on DE Spearman LFC in JURKAT, Overlap@50 in HEPG2, and PDS in RPE1's Systema centroid/MAE comparisons), while the text claims 'consistently outperforms'. No statistical significance testing or multi-seed variance is reported for the headline comparisons beyond per-perturbation std.

The small-effect regime, presented as the paper's central selling point, shows a Pearson-Δ gain of only 1.1% and a PDS *decrease* of 0.4% over TxPert (Table 3); the +28% DES gain is real but headline claims of robustness in this regime are somewhat stronger than the numbers support.

Incremental novelty: individual components (Gumbel-Softmax node selection, Huber losses, cosine alignment) are standard techniques; the contribution is a sensible combination applied to a specific domain rather than a new methodological insight, and the positioning against DEG-aware alternatives like Mejia et al. (2025) is not empirically compared.

Potential circularity between training supervision and evaluation: DEG sets D(p) are derived from statistical tests on ground-truth data and used in both the non-DEG loss and the alignment target (Eqs. 14, 18), while DEG recovery is also the headline evaluation metric. The DEG-threshold sensitivity analysis (Appendix D) partially mitigates this concern, but the tighter coupling between supervision and evaluation relative to baselines deserves more explicit discussion.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: no explicit code/data release statement, and several implementation specifics (hyperparameter values λnon, λalign, temperature τ, threshold T selection protocol, decoder architecture) are deferred or unspecified in the main text; the use of GPT-4o-generated gene descriptions for genes lacking NCBI entries introduces a nondeterministic external dependency.

The motivating Figure 1 (+11% DEG correlation) is a single-perturbation anecdote (UQCRB), which risks overstating the typical magnitude of the mean-collapse correction; aggregate mean-collapse evidence (Appendix F) shows smaller DEG-vs-non-DEG error differentials (3.0% vs 1.8% wMSE).
